contentBlocks.body: Normalization means storing each fact exactly once. A spreadsheet-style orders table that repeats the customer's name and email on every order has three problems, called anomalies: an update anomaly (changing an email means updating many rows, and missing one leaves the data inconsistent), an insert anomaly (you cannot record a customer until they order), and a delete anomaly (deleting a customer's only order deletes the customer too).

The normal forms in one breath: 1NF means every column holds a single value (no comma-separated lists, no repeating column groups like phone1, phone2, phone3). 2NF means non-key columns depend on the whole key, not part of a composite key. 3NF means non-key columns depend only on the key, not on other non-key columns (customer_name depends on customer_email, not on order_id, so it belongs in customers). For CRUD apps, aiming for 3NF and denormalizing deliberately for measured read performance is the usual rule.

contentBlocks.code:
-- M:N: students take many courses; courses have many students.
-- A junction table holds one row per pairing, plus facts about the pairing.
CREATE TABLE enrollments (
  student_id  INT NOT NULL REFERENCES students(id),
  course_id   INT NOT NULL REFERENCES courses(id),
  enrolled_at DATETIME2 NOT NULL,
  grade       CHAR(2) NULL,
  CONSTRAINT PK_enrollments PRIMARY KEY (student_id, course_id)  -- no duplicate pairings
);
CREATE INDEX IX_enrollments_course ON enrollments (course_id);    -- for "students in course X"

contentBlocks.body: EF Core maps these directly: a navigation collection plus a foreign key property gives a 1:N relationship, and a skip navigation (ICollection<Course> on Student and ICollection<Student> on Course) makes EF create the junction table for you. Model the junction as its own entity as soon as the pairing needs data like enrolled_at or grade.

knowledgeItems.prompt: Normalize a flat orders export into customers and orders tables. Customers are identified by email and get ids 1, 2, 3, ... in order of first appearance; the first name seen for an email wins. Return { customers: [{ id, email, name }], orders: [{ id, customerId, total }] } with orders in input order. This is what `INSERT INTO customers ... SELECT DISTINCT` followed by an `INSERT INTO orders ... JOIN customers ON email` migration does.
How should a many-to-many relationship between students and courses be stored?

choices: A comma-separated course_ids column on students
A junction table enrollments(student_id, course_id) with a composite primary key
course1_id, course2_id, course3_id columns on students
payload.answer: A junction table enrollments(student_id, course_id) with a composite primary key
payload.explanation: Each row is one pairing, both columns are foreign keys, and the composite key prevents duplicates. Lists in a column break 1NF and cannot be indexed or constrained.

knowledgeItems.prompt: Which table gets the foreign key in a one-to-many relationship?

payload.text: In a 1:N relationship such as customer to orders, the foreign key column goes on the ____ side (orders.customer_id).

knowledgeItems.prompt: orders_flat stores customer_email on every order. A customer changes their email and only some rows get updated. Which anomaly is this?

payload.explanation: The same fact is stored in many places, so an update can leave copies disagreeing. Storing the email once in customers removes the problem.
